input.question: when you're sick, why do symptoms seem worse at night / when trying to sleep?
input.ground_truth: One of the mechanisms at work is the cortisol level. Cortisol is a steroid hormone your body produces, that (among very many other things) suppresses your immune system. But the Cortisol levels vary during the course of a day. As you might have guessed, the concentration of cortisol in your blood decreases during the day and reaches lower levels in the late evening and night. So basically your symptoms get worse, because there is less immunosuppressive Cortisol to fight the inflammation, which leads to more swelling and stronger pain signals being sent.

Okay! Let’s imagine your body is like a house, and when you get sick, little germs are trying to make trouble inside.

At night, when you’re trying to sleep, your body doesn’t have as many fun things to think about (like playing or watching TV). So, you start to notice how you feel more—like if your throat is scratchy or your head hurts.

Also, when you’re lying down, mucus (that’s the stuff that’s runny or stuffy in your nose) can feel heavier and make you cough more. Plus, your body tries to fix itself when you sleep, so you might feel a bit more achy as your body sends out its helper cells.

So, at night, you notice your sickness more because you’re quiet, still, and your body is working hard to get better!
